{{short description|Optical law in astrophysics}}
'''Kramers' opacity law''' describes the [[opacity (optics)|opacity]] of a medium in terms of the ambient [[density]] and [[temperature]], assuming that the opacity is dominated by [[ionization|bound-free absorption]] (the absorption of light during ionization of a bound [[electron]]) or [[free-free absorption]] (the absorption of light when scattering a free ion, inverse of ''bremsstrahlung'').<ref>Phillips (1999), p. 92.</ref> It is often used to model [[radiative transfer]], particularly in [[stellar atmosphere]]s.<ref>Carroll (1996), p. 274–276.</ref> The relation is named after the [[Dutch people|Dutch]] [[physicist]] [[Hendrik Kramers]], who first derived the form in 1923.<ref>H.A. Kramers (1927). "La diffusion de la lumiere par les atomes". ''Atti Cong. Intern. Fisici'' (Transactions of Volta Centenary Congress) in Como. '''2''': 545–57.</ref><ref name="Carroll274">Carroll (1996), p. 274.</ref>

The general functional form of the opacity law is <math>\bar{\kappa}\propto\rho</math> <math>T^{-7/2},</math> where 
:<math>\bar{\kappa}</math> is the resulting average opacity ((kg/m<sup>3</sup>)<sup>−1</sup>/m), 
:<math>\rho</math> is the density and 
:<math>T</math> the temperature of the medium.
Often the overall opacity is inferred from observations, and this form of the relation describes how changes in the density or temperature (highly non-linear) will affect the opacity.

==Calculation==

The specific forms for bound-free and free-free absorption are:

* Bound-free<math display="block">
\bar{\kappa}_\text{bf}=4.34\times10^{25}\frac{g_\text{bf}}{t}\cdot Z(1+X)\cdot\frac{\rho}{\rm g/cm^3}\left(\frac{T}{\rm K}\right)^{-7/2}{\rm\,cm^2\,g^{-1}},</math>
* [[Bremsstrahlung|Free-free]]<math display="block">
\bar{\kappa}_\text{ff} = 3.68 \times 10^{22} g_\text{ff} \cdot(1-Z)(1+X)\cdot \frac{\rho}{\mathrm{g/cm^3
}} \left(\frac{T}{\rm K}\right)^{-7/2} \mathrm{cm^2 \, g^{-1}}.</math>
By classical [[Thomson scattering|electron-scattering (Thomson)]] opacity depends on H-ion concentration alone: <math display="block">\bar{\kappa}_\mathrm{es}=0.2(1+X)\mathrm{\,cm^2\,g^{-1}}=0.02(1+X)\mathrm{\,m^2\, kg^{-1}}
</math>[[Compton scattering]] of electrons occurs at higher photon energy.

Here, <math>g_\text{bf}</math> and <math>g_\text{ff}</math> are the [[Gaunt factor]]s of circa 1 (quantum-mechanical correction terms) associated with bound-free and free-free transitions respectively. The <math>t</math> is an additional correction factor, typically having a value between 1 and 100. The opacity depends on the number density of electrons and ions in the medium, described by the fractional abundance (by mass): 
* of elements heavier than [[helium]], <math>Z,</math> 
* and of [[hydrogen]], <math>X.</math><ref name="Carroll274"/>
With only helium present (and classical behaviour) <math>\bar{\kappa}_\text{ff}</math> is proportional to mass density and <math>T^{-3.5},</math> valid also for <math>\bar{\kappa}_\text{bf}</math> in lithium etc. medium.
